hero.title: Haloalkanes & Haloarenes — Organic Chemistry's Reactive Stars
hero.hook: Replace one hydrogen in a hydrocarbon with a halogen (F, Cl, Br, I) and you get a haloalkane — one of the most reactive and useful organic compound classes. From PVC pipes to anaesthetics to pesticides, haloalkanes are everywhere. And they're worth 5–6 marks in your boards.

hook_section.scenario: Chloroform (CHCl₃) was used as an early anaesthetic. DDT (a chlorinated compound) wiped out malaria-carrying mosquitoes. Freons (chlorofluorocarbons) became the go-to refrigerants — until we discovered they were destroying the ozone layer. The same reactive C–X bond that makes haloalkanes useful also makes them dangerous. Understanding why requires knowing their reactions.
hook_section.bridge: Haloalkanes undergo two key reaction types: Nucleophilic Substitution (SN1 and SN2) and Elimination. The mechanism depends on the structure of the haloalkane and the nature of the reagent. This is the core of Chapter 10.
hook_section.punchline: The C–X bond is polar (C⁺–X⁻). Nucleophiles attack the electron-deficient carbon. That's the key to all their reactions.

concept_section.analogy: Think of a haloalkane as a lock (the carbon with halogen) and nucleophiles as keys. In SN2, the key goes in the back while the old occupant leaves from the front — one step, inversion. In SN1, the occupant leaves first, creating an open door (carbocation), and then any key can enter — two steps, racemisation. The structure of the lock determines which mechanism dominates.
concept_section.principle: SN2: one step, bimolecular, back-side attack, inversion of configuration. Favoured by primary haloalkanes + strong nucleophiles. SN1: two steps, unimolecular, carbocation intermediate, racemisation. Favoured by tertiary haloalkanes + weak nucleophiles/polar solvents.
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each reaction type to explore 👇

reveals.question: 🔄 SN2 vs SN1 — when does each occur?
reveals.answer: SN2: primary haloalkane + strong nucleophile (OH⁻, CN⁻) + polar aprotic solvent → one step, inversion. SN1: tertiary haloalkane + weak nucleophile + polar protic solvent → two steps, carbocation intermediate, racemisation.

reveals.question: 🌿 Elimination reaction?
reveals.answer: Haloalkane + strong base (KOH/alcohol) → alkene (Zaitsev's rule: more substituted alkene preferred). Competes with substitution. High temperature favours elimination; low temperature favours substitution.

reveals.question: 🌀 Optical isomerism in haloalkanes?
reveals.answer: If the carbon bearing the halogen has 4 different groups → chiral centre → enantiomers possible. SN2 gives inversion (Walden inversion). SN1 gives racemic mixture (equal R and S). Key exam topic.

reveals.question: 🌍 Haloarenes — reactivity difference?
reveals.answer: Halogen attached to benzene ring (haloarenes like chlorobenzene) is much less reactive than haloalkanes. The C–X bond has partial double bond character (resonance) — shorter and stronger. Nucleophilic substitution is very difficult for haloarenes.

points: C–X bond polarity: C⁺–X⁻ makes carbon susceptible to nucleophilic attack
SN2: primary substrate, strong nucleophile, one step, inversion of configuration
SN1: tertiary substrate, two steps, carbocation intermediate, racemisation
Elimination: strong base + haloalkane → alkene; Zaitsev's rule (more substituted product)
Haloarenes: less reactive due to resonance; C–Cl bond shorter/stronger than in haloalkanes

exam_questions.question: Explain SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with one example each. Why is tertiary haloalkane more reactive in SN1 but less reactive in SN2 compared to primary?
Why is chlorobenzene less reactive than chloromethane towards nucleophilic substitution?

quiz.q: Which substrate undergoes SN2 reaction most readily?
quiz.exp: SN2 requires back-side attack. Primary haloalkanes have least steric hindrance — the nucleophile can approach easily. Tertiary haloalkanes are too bulky for SN2.

quiz.q: SN1 reaction proceeds through which intermediate?
quiz.exp: In SN1, the leaving group departs first (step 1) forming a carbocation intermediate. The nucleophile then attacks the carbocation (step 2). Tertiary carbocations are most stable (most substituted).

quiz.q: Chlorobenzene on reaction with NaOH at 300°C gives:
quiz.exp: Chlorobenzene reacts with NaOH at high temperature and pressure to give phenol (C₆H₅OH). This requires forcing conditions because C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene has partial double bond character.

quiz.q: What is formed when CH₃CH₂Cl reacts with KOH in alcohol?
quiz.exp: KOH in alcohol acts as a strong base and promotes elimination (not substitution). The product is ethene (CH₂=CH₂). KOH in water promotes substitution to give alcohol.

flipcards.front: What is the IUPAC name of CHCl₃?
SN2 — which configuration does the product have?
flipcards.back: Inverted configuration (Walden inversion) — attack occurs from opposite side to leaving group

flipcards.front: Why are haloarenes less reactive than haloalkanes?
flipcards.back: Resonance between halogen lone pair and benzene ring gives C–X bond partial double bond character — shorter and stronger
More substituted (more stable) alkene is the major product

flipcards.front: SN1 gives what type of mixture?
flipcards.back: Racemic mixture (equal amounts of R and S enantiomers) — carbocation is planar, attack from both sides equally likely
SN1: polar protic (water, alcohol). SN2: polar aprotic (acetone, DMSO)
